summary: Beijing drafts limits on exporting its biggest AI models, growth figures arrive Monday, and Duolingo starts teaching Shanghainese.
body: The biggest tech story is Beijing's draft list of technologies that would need a licence to leave China (see the World tab for the global angle). It would cover the core parts of China's largest AI models, such as their weights and code, plus some AI chip designs [^1][^2]. AP notes that models from Moonshot (Kimi K3) and Alibaba (Qwen 3.8-Max) are above the 2-trillion-parameter line, though the draft names no companies [^2]. Chinese firms could still sell to foreign users through apps and websites, and open-source code is exempt [^1]. Comments close November 15 [^1].

Tomorrow, Monday, China publishes third-quarter growth figures along with September retail sales, a rough measure of how much households spend [^3]. A Reuters poll of 50 economists expects 4.4% growth from a year earlier, just under the government's 4.5% to 5% target range, with the long property slump still weighing on spending [^3].

In daily life, Duolingo launched lessons in Shanghainese, a dialect spoken by about 10 million people that has faded as Mandarin spread through schools and media; China is the app's fastest-growing market [^4]. And an AI-generated girl group on Xiaohongshu (RedNote) drew mockery and criticism after announcing that one virtual member was pregnant and taking leave. Critics said it treated women's health as entertainment; the creators, who say they are students, said they had been harassed [^5]. My read: virtual idols are becoming common online in China, and so are fights over what they should be allowed to pretend.

reads.summary: A first-person account from a Qingdao car saleswoman targeted by fake AI videos: what platforms and police did, and why many women feel they have little protection.
